metadata.assigned_reading: Ohlhaver, Weyl, and Buterin, Decentralized Society: Finding Web3's Soul
metadata.note: The lesson has no check, worked, practice, answers or review slides (it predates docs/lesson-standard.md), so no slide is required by the coverage decision; the questions cover the visible slides on what tokens do not guarantee, standards, communities, minting, metadata, soulbound tokens, the Frosties rug pull and chokepoints. The two hidden DAO re-entrancy slides get no questions. Reading questions test lesson claims on visible slides that Ohlhaver, Weyl and Buterin (cited on the Soulbound Tokens and Analyst Implications notes) support; the reading was not re-fetched.

lectures.title: Token-Based Communities & NFTs in Practice - lesson synthesis
Token-Based Communities & NFTs in Practice - reading synthesis

questions.question_stem: A museum says its NFTs represent ownership of physical artworks. What can an analyst take from the chain itself?
questions.correct_answer: Token ownership and transfers are verified on-chain; legal ownership of the artwork and the wallet holder's identity are not.
incorrect_answers: Token ownership and legal title move together, so a transfer hands over the artwork's title and only custody is left.
The token's history verifies the museum's claim about the artwork, so the chain itself settles who owns the piece.
The wallet holder's identity is verified along with the token, so the token's owner is the artwork's legal owner.
questions.explanation: The slide separates what the chain verifies (signatures, balance changes, contract execution, event logs) from what it does not (file contents, legal ownership, identity of the wallet holder, meaning of metadata).

questions.question_stem: A game needs one contract for a fungible currency, identical consumables and unique skins. Which standard fits?
questions.correct_answer: ERC-1155, which tracks a balance per (address, ID) pair, so one contract holds fungible and unique items.
incorrect_answers: ERC-20, which tracks a balance per address, so one contract holds currency, consumables and skins as amounts.
ERC-721, which tracks one owner per token ID, so one contract gives each currency unit and skin an ID.
Separate ERC-20 and ERC-721 contracts, because no single standard tracks fungible and unique items together.
questions.explanation: The table lists ERC-1155 as the multi-token standard: balance per (address, ID) pair, amounts per ID, typical use gaming inventory.

questions.question_stem: Why is choosing a token standard more than an implementation detail?
questions.correct_answer: It is an architectural commitment that constrains every wallet, market, and indexer built on the token.
incorrect_answers: It sets the validator fee market and transaction order, which decide how fast transfers of the token confirm.
It sets the copyright terms and tax treatment of the token, which decide how off-chain disputes are settled.
It sets the compiler and node networking format, which decide how the token's contract code is run on the nodes.
questions.explanation: The slide's warning: standard choice is an architectural commitment that constrains every downstream wallet, market, and indexer.

questions.question_stem: An NFT's tokenURI points to an HTTP URL on the issuer's own server. What is the integrity concern?
questions.correct_answer: The token stays on-chain, but the server operator can change or delete the linked content silently.
incorrect_answers: The token becomes invalid once the server goes down, because ownership is stored in the issuer's database.
The file's address changes when the issuer edits it, so every holder must re-mint the token.
The token's history is hidden from indexers, since an HTTP pointer replaces the Transfer events on-chain.
questions.explanation: A location address names a server, so the operator can change or delete the content; a content address is a hash, so changing the file changes the address.

questions.question_stem: A token-gated Discord admits a wallet that holds the token. What does the gate enforce, and what does it leave off-chain?
questions.correct_answer: The gate enforces entry by token ownership; communication, culture, and moderation stay in the off-chain social layer.
incorrect_answers: The gate enforces moderation as well as entry, because the token contract assigns roles and removes members.
The gate enforces that each wallet maps to one real participant, so moderators need no further check on joiners.
The gate enforces culture and norms through token weight, so members holding more tokens set each channel's rules.
questions.explanation: Access control is enforced on-chain; communication, culture and norms, and moderation and curation sit in the off-chain social layer.

questions.question_stem: A project gives members an NFT as a badge and a fungible token as a treasury budget. How is this design classified?
questions.correct_answer: As a hybrid: the NFT is identity and the fungible token is budget, so each token controls a different thing.
incorrect_answers: As a pure DAO, because the fungible token carries the votes and the NFT is only a label for member profile status.
As a membership NFT, because the badge decides admission and the fungible token adds nothing to it.
As a social token, because one fungible asset signals status and holds the treasury budget for them.
questions.explanation: The slide says the patterns mix freely and names the hybrid: NFT = identity, fungible = budget.

questions.question_stem: Why is minting more than creating a token?
questions.correct_answer: The minter controls who can mint, how many tokens exist, and what metadata each token points to.
incorrect_answers: The minter controls only the token's display name, leaving supply and access to marketplace rules.
The minter controls the price of later sales, while the supply is set by how validators order blocks.
The minter controls the wallet's display, while the token standard fixes supply and who may mint.
questions.explanation: The slide lists three controls for the minter: who can mint, how many exist, and what metadata the token points to.

questions.question_stem: A contract declares an EIP-2981 royalty, yet a marketplace completes a resale without paying it. Why is that possible?
questions.correct_answer: The contract only declares the recipient and basis points; whether a marketplace pays the royalty varies.
incorrect_answers: Ethereum consensus enforces royalties on every resale, so the network should have rejected the unpaid sale.
The royalty field passes the creator's copyright to the buyer, so no payment is owed on later resales.
The creator can reverse the resale through the same standard, so the marketplace owes nothing before then.
questions.explanation: The slide describes royalty signaling: the contract declares recipient and basis points, and marketplace enforcement varies.

questions.question_stem: Frosties' operators scattered the proceeds across several wallets. What let investigators link them to their planned second project, Embers?
questions.correct_answer: Wallet reuse: every transfer was publicly recorded on-chain, so the same operator wallets tied the two projects together.
incorrect_answers: Website records: the operators' deactivated site and deleted Discord showed who ran both projects before the arrest.
Contract bugs: the Frosties mint contract exposed the operators' identities to every holder once the sale sold out.
Marketplace reports: the scattering through multiple wallets was flagged by the sites that had listed the NFTs.
questions.explanation: The slide names wallet reuse as the forensic link and says every transfer was publicly recorded on-chain, even when proceeds were routed through multiple wallets.

questions.question_stem: A dApp fails for most users when its RPC provider has an outage, while Ethereum L1 keeps producing blocks. What does this show?
questions.correct_answer: RPC providers, bridges, and oracles reintroduce single points of failure above a decentralized L1 chain.
incorrect_answers: L1 consensus depends on the largest RPC providers, so an outage there pauses block production.
Token standards define RPC failover, so the dApp's tokens are lost until the provider's servers resync.
Bridges and oracles share L1 consensus security, so an outage in either means the whole base chain has forked.
questions.explanation: The slide says that although L1 is decentralized, RPC providers, bridges and oracles reintroduce single points of failure.

questions.question_stem: An analyst finds a soulbound token on a wallet. What does the transfer lock establish about the holder?
questions.correct_answer: Only that the wallet holds it; the person is bound only if that person controls the private key.
incorrect_answers: That a real person holds it, since the contract verifies a person's identity before it locks the token.
That the recipient still holds it, since the lock stops a key sale from moving the credential elsewhere.
That one person holds one token, since the issuer checks each wallet maps to a single real person.
questions.explanation: The slide's open problem: non-transferability binds the credential to a wallet, not a person; it holds only if the person controls the private key (a key sale is a credential sale). Ohlhaver, Weyl and Buterin likewise treat a Soul as an account that need not map to one person.

questions.question_stem: Who creates a soulbound token, and what can its recipient do with it?
questions.correct_answer: An issuer such as an institution, DAO or peer signs the mint; the recipient can hold and use it but not sell it.
incorrect_answers: The recipient signs the mint for themselves; they can hold and use it, and can pass it on once to a new wallet.
An issuer such as an institution, DAO or peer signs the mint; the recipient can hold it and sell it on issuer approval.
A marketplace signs the mint for the recipient; they can hold and display it but cannot use it for access.
questions.explanation: The slide's flow: an issuer signs the mint, transfer functions are locked, and the wallet can hold, display and use the token for access but not sell or transfer it. The reading frames SBTs as attestations issued by institutions, DAOs and peers.

questions.question_stem: An analyst notes that SBTs and on-chain attestations make verifiable credential records with no central issuing authority. How should the analyst read that capability?
questions.correct_answer: It enables legitimate and adversarial coordination with the same mechanism, so both uses must be weighed.
incorrect_answers: It makes credentials trustworthy, so an on-chain attestation can be treated as proof of the holder's identity.
It limits adversarial use, because a record with no central issuer cannot be turned to a harmful use.
It matters only to legitimate users, since adversarial parties need a central authority to issue credentials.
questions.explanation: The closing line of the slide: each capability cuts in two directions, enabling legitimate and adversarial coordination with the same mechanism. The reading likewise warns that SBT infrastructure can support cooperation or surveillance and exclusion.
